item.title: Public Goods and Common-Pool Resources: Why Voluntary Provision Fails
item.description: Public goods are non-excludable and non-rival; common-pool resources are rival but hard to exclude. Both make free riding and overuse the default. This article puts the Samuelson condition, the voluntary-provision gap and common-pool quotas into one account, and shows which part government, clubs and community rules can each solve.

item.title: Three Phillips Curves: Wages, Expectations and Supply Shocks
item.description: The Phillips curve is not one line with a fixed slope. The wage-bargaining version trades inflation against unemployment; the expectations-augmented version removes anticipated inflation from the trade-off; the supply-shock version shifts the whole curve. Only the three together explain why the same unemployment rate can come with high or low inflation.

item.title: Balance-Sheet Runoff and the Rate Corridor: How Central-Bank Assets Transmit
item.description: Quantitative tightening is not simply withdrawing liquidity. Bond runoff on the asset side, reserves and overnight reverse repos on the liability side, and the corridor's floor and ceiling jointly determine whether short rates stay controlled. This article separates the T-account, reserve supply and demand, and the three corridor segments, then calculates a runoff shock.

item.title: Who Pays the Tariff: Intermediate Goods, Rules of Origin and Value Chains
item.description: The legal tariff payer is the importer, but the economic burden is shared by consumers, importers, exporters and upstream suppliers. Intermediate goods, rules of origin and value chains turn a simple tariff line into an effective rate of protection, compliance cost and double taxation. This article uses the effective-protection formula and a three-country value-chain example to separate who really pays.

item.title: Balance-of-Payments Crises: Reserves, Capital Flows and Exchange Regimes
item.description: A balance-of-payments crisis is not the trade deficit itself, but a maturity mismatch among usable reserves, short-term external debt and capital flows. A fixed rate turns exchange-rate risk into reserve risk; a float turns reserve risk into price risk. This article uses reserve-cover ratios and a sudden-stop example to separate the trigger sequence.

item.title: Platform Entry Barriers: Data, Network Effects and Interoperability
item.description: Platform entry barriers are not just 'many users'. Network effects, data feedback, switching costs and multi-homing jointly determine whether a new platform can reach minimum viable scale. This article puts two-sided subsidies, the data flywheel and interoperability duties into one entry account, and explains why antitrust looks at contestability rather than market share alone.

item.title: Housing Affordability: Land, Commuting and Zoning
item.description: Housing affordability is not one price-to-income ratio; it is the combined result of land supply, zoning density, commuting cost and local public finance. This article links developable land, floor-area ratio, commuting radius and the affordable range, explaining why the same income buys very different housing in different parts of a city.

item.title: System Costs of the Energy Transition: Grids, Storage and Capacity Markets
item.description: Falling levelised costs of wind and solar do not make the whole power system cheaper. Intermittent supply needs grid expansion, storage, balancing and capacity backup, and these system costs are not in the module price. This article puts LCOE, system cost and capacity markets into one account and calculates the true cost of a 60% renewable system.

item.title: Scaling Behavioural Interventions: When Defaults Cross the Line
item.description: Defaults, salience and social norms can work in randomised trials, but that does not mean they survive scale-up. This article puts effect size, reach, implementation cost and ethical boundaries into one account, explaining why opt-out defaults raise participation while potentially denying choice without users' knowledge.

item.title: Law Enforcement and Market Trust: The Testable Part of Comparative Institutions
item.description: Law promotes market trust not through the quality of statutes but through clear property rights, enforceable contracts and calculable breach costs. This article uses transaction costs, enforcement costs and trust substitution to open the 'good institutions, fast growth' black box and keep only the testable part.

item.title: Global Spillovers from China's Manufacturing Upgrade: Intermediates, Demand and Rules
item.description: China's manufacturing upgrade is not simply 'exporting more final goods'; it changes global production networks through intermediates, capital goods, demand spillovers and rule participation. This article separates forward linkages, backward linkages and demand spillovers into three calculable channels, showing who gains, who adjusts and who faces competitive pressure.

item.title: 2020 fiscal stimulus across countries: why multipliers diverged
item.description: The US, Germany, Japan and the euro area all expanded fiscal policy in 2020, yet output responded differently. The difference was not how much was spent but the composition, saving behaviour and supply constraints.

item.title: The EU ETS in 2022: Cap, Carbon Price and Border Adjustment
item.description: The EU ETS cap was 1.528 billion allowances in 2022, about 43 million below the prior year; auction prices reached €97.51 in February and €57.91 in March. Put the cap, auctions and free allocation on one chain to see that the carbon price is not an administrative price but the price of allowance scarcity.

item.title: Korea and Argentina: institutional divergence under the same external shock
item.description: The 1997 Asian crisis and the 2001 Argentine crisis both began with external financing stress, yet the outcomes diverged. Exchange-rate regime, bank supervision and fiscal space determined how the same shock became different output losses.

item.title: When Financial Functions Fail: Intermediation Cost Above Coordination Benefit
item.description: The financial system exists to lower search, assessment, monitoring and settlement costs between savers and investors. When fragmentation, information asymmetry or regulatory friction push intermediation cost above coordination benefit, financial functions fail: cash sits idle while projects cannot borrow. This article uses a loan intermediation-cost account to separate the failure points of six functions.

item.title: Constraints on Credit Creation: Capital, Liquidity and Loan Demand
item.description: Banks do not simply 'take deposits and lend'; they create credit under three constraints: capital, liquidity and loan demand. This article uses a T-account and a capital-ratio example to explain why the same deposit lets one bank lend 90 yuan and another only 60.

item.title: Ample Reserves and the Floor System: How the Corridor Works
item.description: Under an ample-reserves framework, the central bank no longer fine-tunes rates through scarce reserves and open-market operations; it sets a floor with the reserve rate and ON RRP rate, letting market rates run inside a corridor. This article uses a reserve supply-demand table to explain why the floor system needs reverse repos and when it fails.

item.title: Three Messages in the Yield Curve: Expectations, Risk and Liquidity
item.description: An inverted yield curve is often read as a recession signal, but the curve carries at least three messages: future rate expectations, term risk premium and liquidity premium. Separating them tells whether inversion reflects tight policy or risk repricing.

item.title: Accounting Estimates and Accruals: Where Earnings Quality Shows
item.description: The same cash flow can produce very different net income under different depreciation lives, bad-debt provisions and warranty accruals. Accruals are not fraud, but they give management judgement room; to read earnings quality, trace where accruals go and whether they reverse.

item.title: Three-Statement Articulation: Balance Sheet, Income Statement and Cash Flow
item.description: Net income from the income statement enters retained earnings on the balance sheet, and the cash change from the cash-flow statement enters cash and equivalents. A few accounts link the three statements; when articulation fails, classification, consolidation scope or estimates are usually the cause.

item.title: Buybacks versus Dividends: Same Cash Return, Different Signals
item.description: Dividends are a stable cash commitment; buybacks are flexible capital allocation. Both reduce cash, but buybacks also change share count and per-share metrics. Do not read buybacks only through EPS accretion; check price, funding source and whether they offset equity-compensation dilution.

item.title: Longevity Risk and Annuities: Converting Savings into Lifetime Income
item.description: The point of an annuity is not high return but converting uncertain lifespan into certain income. It pools mortality risk across survivors but shifts inflation, fee and counterparty risk to the policyholder.

item.title: Offshore Dollar Funding: Swaps, FX Swaps and Rollover Risk
item.description: Offshore institutions need dollars but lack U.S. deposit insurance and the discount window; they obtain dollars through FX swaps, offshore deposits and central-bank swap lines. When dollars tighten, swap basis widens and rollover becomes difficult, transmitting stress back onshore.

item.title: Stablecoin Reserves, Pegs and Runs: Is It a Bank?
item.description: A stablecoin promises one coin for one dollar and holds reserves to defend the peg. It compresses deposit-reserve-redemption into an on-chain liability but lacks deposit insurance and a lender of last resort; reserve quality, maturity mismatch and redemption speed decide whether it runs.

item.title: Wholesale Funding Runs: LCR, NSFR and Fire Sales
item.description: Wholesale funding is not deposits, but it is more sensitive: repos, interbank certificates, commercial paper and bonds can stop rolling instantly under stress. LCR covers 30-day survival and NSFR the one-year structure; a bank can pass both and still run on collateral discounts and concentration.

item.title: Client Asset Custody: Segregation, Rehypothecation and Institution Failure
item.description: Client assets are not the institution's own assets; custody is about segregation and traceability. If client assets are commingled, rehypothecated or lent to counterparties, they become general claims in a failure. The longer the custody chain, the harder the recovery.

item.title: The US move to T+1 in 2024: the chain reaction of a shorter settlement cycle
item.description: Settlement moving from T+2 to T+1 looks like saving one day, but it reorders FX, funding, securities lending and operational time zones. The real question is not whether a trade can settle, but whether the whole chain can match cash and securities in a shorter window.

item.title: Commercial paper in 2008 and 2020: how haircuts froze short-term funding
item.description: The commercial paper market froze twice in crises through the same mechanism: investors refused to roll over, haircuts rose and borrowers were forced to sell assets. Central-bank facilities can supply liquidity, but cannot replace solvency.

item.title: The 2022 UK LDI Crisis: Margin Spirals and Pensions
item.description: After the September 2022 mini-budget, 30-year gilt yields rose more than 270 basis points in weeks, forcing leveraged LDI funds to sell gilts for collateral. Put yields, collateral and pension liabilities on one timeline to see how non-bank leverage became a systemic risk.

item.title: Silk, Silver and Tribute: Money and Governance in Eurasian Trade Networks
item.description: The Silk Road was not a single road but a network of oases, steppe routes, seaports and tribute missions. Silk, silver and tribute gifts served monetary, diplomatic and governance functions at different nodes; understanding the network explains the rise and fall of Eurasian trade.

item.title: From the Corn Laws to Free Trade: The Ledger of British Policy Debate
item.description: The Corn Laws were not simply landlords versus manufacturers; they were a distributional ledger of land rents, wages, industrial profits and food security. Repeal lowered food prices and reshaped Britain's political coalitions and global trade.

item.title: The Socialist Calculation Debate: Prices, Planning and Information
item.description: The calculation debate of the 1920s-30s was not an ideological slogan but an information problem: without market prices, can planners know where resources should go? Mises and Hayek stressed dispersed information; Lange proposed simulated prices and trial-and-error rules.

item.title: From Marginal Utility to Welfare Economics: Pareto, Pigou and Arrow
item.description: Welfare economics starts from utility and asks what counts as a good allocation. Pareto efficiency, Pigouvian externalities and Arrow's impossibility theorem define the boundaries of efficiency, equity and collective choice.

item.title: The Resource Curse in Africa and the Middle East: Institutions, Rents and Conflict
item.description: Resource abundance does not guarantee growth: rents concentrate, institutions get captured and conflict gets financed. Africa and the Middle East show that the resource curse is not geological destiny but a result of institutions, rent distribution and external shocks.

item.title: Historical Echoes of Digital Money: From Notes and Bills to CBDC
item.description: Digital money is not entirely new: notes, bills, bank deposits and credit cards all did the same thing, turning money from an object into a transferable accounting claim. CBDC differs in the issuer being the central bank, the liability being a central-bank liability, and programmability.

item.title: The Origins of Insurance: Marine Insurance, Mutual Aid and Actuarial Science
item.description: Insurance did not begin with risk aversion but with maritime merchants sharing losses on ships and cargo. Marine insurance, mutual societies and life annuities turned random losses into priceable premiums; actuarial science made mortality and the law of large numbers commercial foundations.

item.title: The Investment Policy Statement: Writing Objectives, Constraints and Rebalancing into Rules
item.description: An investment policy statement is not compliance decoration; it writes down why you invest, how much risk you can bear and when to adjust, in executable rules. Without one, portfolios drift with emotion, hype and short-term performance.

item.title: The Macro Scenario Tree: Probabilities for Growth, Inflation and Policy Paths
item.description: A macro forecast is not a point but a scenario tree: growth, inflation and policy each have paths, and probabilities determine expected value and tail risk. Writing scenarios as a tree shows where a forecast can go wrong.

item.title: Industry Map: A Diligence Checklist from Value Chain to Capital Returns
item.description: Industry research starts not with a story but with a map: who is upstream, who is downstream, where profit pools sit and why capital returns differ. Overlaying the value chain, entry barriers and capital intensity shows whether a company earns from industry structure or a temporary cycle.

item.title: Factor Crowding: When the Same Alpha Becomes Collective Risk
item.description: Factor crowding is not simply many investors using the same factor; it is many using the same trade to express it. When leverage, shorts and liquidity align, one redemption or deleveraging can reverse factor returns instantly.

item.title: Hedge Ratio: Minimum Variance, Basis Risk and Tail Protection
item.description: A hedge ratio is not '100% or nothing'; it is how much to hedge, with which instrument and how much basis risk to bear. The minimum-variance ratio cuts volatility but may sacrifice return; tail protection needs non-linear tools, not simply more shorts.

item.title: Luck versus Skill: Evidence from Multi-Period Excess Returns
