item.description: This article puts "event window", "leak" and "placebo" on the same judgment chain, unifying the caliber first, and then discussing the mechanism and boundaries.

item.title: Data Lineage: Revisions, Missingness, and Pipeline Audits
item.description: This article puts "data lineage", "revision" and "deletion" on the same judgment chain, unifying the caliber first, and then discussing the mechanism and boundaries.

item.title: Reproduction of a paper: from abstract to code
item.description: This article puts "paper reproduction", "abstract" and "code" on the same judgment chain, unifying the caliber first, and then discussing the mechanism and boundaries.

item.title: Anscombe’s quartet and the malt tax: regression specification errors
item.description: Four datasets can share means, variances and a regression coefficient while looking completely different. Anscombe’s quartet is a warning: plot before regressing; the same coefficient does not make the model right.

item.title: The 2008 Oregon Medicaid Lottery: Random Assignment and Policy Evaluation
item.description: In 2008 Oregon used a lottery to select about 30,000 people from a waiting list of nearly 90,000, and about 10,000 enrolled. An administrative necessity became a randomised experiment, letting researchers estimate the causal effect of Medicaid on visits, prescriptions and debt.

item.title: FDA approval event studies: windows and leakage
item.description: FDA approval is a classic information event, but the approval date, leakage timing and market expectations all enter returns. A wider window captures other news; a narrower window may miss anticipatory reaction.

item.title: FRED vintage replication: how revisions change conclusions
item.description: The same quarter’s GDP can differ by several percentage points between advance, second and final estimates. Backtesting decisions with final data overstates what was available; vintage data is the only way to replicate "what was known then".

item.title: Contracts, Specific Assets and Organizational Boundaries: A Transaction-Cost Ledger
item.description: Markets, long-term contracts and internal organization are not three ideologies; they are three ways of handling transaction costs. The more specific the asset, the easier each party is locked in, and the more a sunk investment can be eroded by later renegotiation. Put contracting, monitoring, enforcement and bureaucratic costs on one ledger to decide whether a transaction belongs in the market, in a contract or inside a firm.

item.title: China's External Balance and Value-Chain Position: Reading the External Ledger
item.description: A country's external ledger is more than a trade surplus. The current account equals saving minus investment, and net foreign assets are also changed by exchange rates and valuation; gross exports contain imported inputs, so only the value-added share shows what a country actually creates. Put saving-investment, value-added trade, net foreign assets and reserve cover on one ledger to read how China connects to the global economy.

item.title: Financial Intermediation and Direct Financing: How Savings Become Investment
item.description: Finance is not money breeding money. It rearranges scattered savings, risks and maturities and sends them to projects that need funding. Direct financing puts users of funds in front of investors; indirect financing has banks and other intermediaries collect deposits first and lend afterwards. The two routes allocate cost, information and risk differently.

item.title: Rate Conventions and Credit Spreads: Different Labels for the Same Price of Money
item.description: The same 5% can be a nominal rate, a real rate, a coupon, a yield to maturity or an annual percentage rate. The difference is not a decimal point. Separate inflation, compounding frequency, credit and liquidity premia before comparing the cost of two funding options.

item.title: Insurance Pricing and Pension Liabilities: The Ledger of Risk Sharing
item.description: Insurance does not abolish risk; it pools many small-probability, large-loss exposures into a predictable pool. Premium must cover expected claims, expenses and capital, while reserves must cover future benefits. Pensions separate current contributions from future promises; a funding gap is eventually closed by contributions, investment returns or public money.

item.title: Cross-Border Payments and Reserve Currencies: The Plumbing of International Finance
item.description: A cross-border payment is not money “traveling” abroad; it is a chain of bookings across banks, clearing systems, correspondents and FX markets. A reserve currency is special because it serves as payment unit, funding currency and store of value at once. Reserve cover puts exchange-rate stability and import-paying capacity on one table.

item.title: Tokenized Deposits and Stablecoins: The Ledger of Payment Infrastructure
item.description: Stablecoins and tokenized deposits both move “deposits” onto programmable ledgers, but the obligor, reserve assets and redemption rights differ. Safety cannot be read from the on-chain price alone; it depends on reserve cover, redemption order, settlement finality and who bears a run.

item.title: Bank Runs, Leverage and Contagion: A Financial-Stability Stress Test
item.description: Financial stability is not the absence of volatility; it is the system’s ability to keep payments and funding going under stress. A run is a liquidity problem, leverage amplifies losses, and contagion turns one failure into a network event. A stress test separates the three layers and puts them back on one balance sheet.

item.title: Disclosure, Suitability and Conflicts of Interest: Three Regulatory Ledgers
item.description: Financial regulation is not just more forms. Disclosure addresses information asymmetry, suitability addresses the fit between product and client, and conflicts rules address who decides for whom. The three ledgers cover different gaps and cannot substitute for one another. Put client assets, market integrity and firm incentives on one table to judge whether a rule actually protects investors.

item.title: From Aristotle to Aquinas: Wealth, Interest and the Boundaries of Exchange
item.description: Early economic thought was not “ancient economics”; it discussed whether exchange is just, money is natural and interest is legitimate within the frames of household, city and salvation. Aristotle separated livelihood from unlimited acquisition; Aquinas placed usury, the just price and fraud inside medieval theology and law.

item.title: Marx’s Circuit of Capital: From Capital to Socialist Accounting
item.description: Marx treated capital as a movement through changing forms: money buys means of production and labour, production creates commodities, and commodities sell for more money. Surplus value, the organic composition of capital and reproduction schemes were his core tools for explaining profit and crisis.

item.title: The Marginal Revolution: Jevons, Menger and Walras on Exchange
item.description: The marginal revolution shifted economics from “how much is produced” to “how much is one more unit worth”. Jevons, Menger and Walras almost simultaneously found that value comes from marginal utility and equilibrium from exchange ratios; Marshall then turned marginal analysis into a teachable price theory.

item.title: After Keynes: Monetarism, New Classical and New Keynesian Economics
item.description: Keynes brought effective demand, uncertainty and policy space into macroeconomics; postwar debates turned on how potent fiscal policy is, how much money matters, and how expectations change rules. Monetarism, new classical and new Keynesian economics are not three slogans but three models of shocks, expectations and policy response.

item.title: The Great Divergence and Institutional Comparison: Evidence from Regional History
item.description: Why did Western Europe industrialise first in the nineteenth century while other regions did not? The Great Divergence debate puts geography, institutions, colonisation, energy and knowledge networks on one comparative table. This article adds representative experiences from Europe and the Americas, Asia, Africa and the Middle East, then sets out four checks for institutional comparison.

item.title: From Coin to Central Bank: A History of Banking, Insurance and Payments
item.description: Modern financial intermediaries were not designed in one go. Coin, bills, deposits, insurance and pensions solved different problems in different eras: payment, long-distance settlement, risk pooling and old-age support. Central banks acquired note issue, lender-of-last-resort and supervisory functions through crises and wars.

item.title: War Finance and Sovereign Debt: The Ledger of State Capacity
item.description: Sovereign debt is not simply “government borrowing”; it is an intertemporal exchange among war, taxation and credit. The debt ratio depends on interest rates, growth and the primary balance; whether a state can borrow, for how long and in what currency reflects state capacity and credible commitment.

item.title: From Mutual Funds to Indexing and Quant: The Institutionalisation of Investment Thought
item.description: Investment thought expanded from “picking good companies” to portfolios, indices, factors and quant models. Mutual funds made diversification a mass product, index funds made low-cost beta replicable, and factor research decomposed return sources into testable exposures.

item.title: From Macro to Assets: Pricing Growth, Inflation and Policy
item.description: Macro research is not forecasting one GDP number; it links growth, inflation, policy rates and risk premia into an asset-pricing chain. Real rates, earnings expectations and discount rates move separately, and asset prices rearrange; the same macro data mean different things for different assets.

item.title: Industry and Company: Moats and Return on Capital
item.description: Industry research asks where the money comes from and why it persists; company research asks whether a firm can turn industry profit into its own return on capital. A moat is not a brand slogan but a structure that stops competition from eroding returns: network, switching cost, scale, patents and location.

item.title: Earnings Quality: Profit, Cash and Accruals
item.description: Profit is an accounting measure; cash is an economic one. High accruals and low cash conversion can signal aggressive revenue recognition, working-capital bloat or one-off gains; earnings-quality analysis turns profit back into cash and capital and then tests durability.

item.title: Where Strategy Returns Come From: Beta, Factors and Capacity
item.description: Any strategy return can be split into market beta, identifiable factors, genuine alpha and luck. Decomposing the sources shows whether it is replicable and whether capacity and fees will eat it; high return does not equal high skill.

item.title: Hedging and Stress Testing: The Cost of Protection
item.description: Hedging does not remove risk; it changes its shape. Futures lock in a price but give up upside; options pay a premium but keep some upside. Stress testing asks whether protection still works in extreme scenarios.

item.title: Performance Attribution: Where the Return Came From
item.description: Performance attribution splits portfolio-minus-benchmark returns into allocation, selection and interaction: right sectors, right stocks, and their combination. Without attribution, performance is a story; with it, you can judge whether it is repeatable.

item.title: Behavioral Biases and Investment Discipline: Knowing Is Not Doing
item.description: The biggest risk for investors is sometimes not the market but their own behaviour: overtrading, the disposition effect, chasing returns, overconfidence and recency bias. Discipline is not a willpower slogan but an executable process of decision rules, position limits and checklists.

item.title: The Household Balance Sheet: Human Capital, Housing and Pensions
item.description: A household is not just “how much money it has”; it also has future wages, housing, pensions and liabilities. Human capital resembles a bond, housing a local asset, pensions a long-horizon fund; putting them on one sheet shows whether risk is concentrated.

item.title: Responsible Investment and Professional Ethics: Writing Preferences into Portfolios
item.description: Responsible investment is not “doing good earns more”; it turns environmental, social and governance preferences into executable screening, engagement and disclosure rules. Professional ethics put client interests, conflicts and suitability before sales.

item.title: Environmental Capacity and Specialised Markets: Pricing Carbon, Water and Weather
item.description: Environmental capacity is a scarce resource: emission rights, water rights and weather risk can be measured, allocated and traded. Specialised markets turn “who may use how much, who bears weather losses” into prices, but whether prices work depends on caps, monitoring and compliance.

item.title: REITs and Infrastructure: Cash Flow, Leverage and Valuation
item.description: REITs package rental cash flows from real estate into tradable shares; infrastructure funds package long-term cash flows from tolls, networks and power plants into similar structures. Both attract investors with stable cash flow and are constrained by rates, leverage and asset quality.

item.title: Private Funds and Hedge Funds: Fees, Lock-ups and Liquidity
item.description: Private funds and hedge funds sell not a stock but a strategy, a fee schedule and a liquidity arrangement. 2/20 fees, lock-ups, side pockets and redemption gates determine net returns and whether investors can exit in a crisis.

item.title: Retirement Products and Accounts: Annuities, Target-Date Funds and Tax Advantages
item.description: Retirement products solve “will there be cash flow after retirement”; accounts solve “which tax container holds the money”. Annuities turn savings into lifetime income, target-date funds glide allocation with age, and tax-advantaged accounts rearrange contribution and withdrawal timing.

item.title: Regression and Econometrics: Coefficients, Standard Errors and Causality
item.description: Regression gives conditional association, not automatic causation. Coefficient size, standard errors, confidence intervals and model specification jointly determine the strength of a conclusion; shrinking standard errors or piling on controls can manufacture false certainty.

item.title: Forecasting and Machine Learning: Out-of-Sample, Overfitting and Baselines
item.description: A forecasting model is judged out of sample, not on the training set. Baselines, rolling windows, overfitting and multiple comparisons determine whether it is useful; if a complex model loses to a simple baseline, complexity is a cost rather than an advantage.

item.title: Alternative Data and Complex Systems: Signal, Noise and Networks
item.description: Alternative data is not “more data” but data from a different generating process: satellite images, card transactions, job postings, shipping and social text. Complex systems remind us that variables have feedback, thresholds and network contagion, so linear extrapolation often fails.

item.title: Research Reading and Writing: Question, Evidence and Reproduction
item.description: Good research is not “opinion plus data” but a question that can be answered, evidence that can be checked and a conclusion with boundaries. When reading, start with the question and identification, then the conclusion; when writing, make data, method, robustness and limits reproducible.

item.title: Opportunity Cost and Sunk Cost
item.description: Opportunity cost measures the value of the next-best alternative; a sunk cost is already unrecoverable and should not keep driving the next decision.

item.title: Margin and Incentives
item.description: Marginal decisions compare the benefit and cost of one more unit, and incentives change those two quantities.

item.title: Supply, Demand and Equilibrium
item.description: Demand and supply curves relate price and quantity; equilibrium is their intersection, and movements along a curve differ from shifts of the curve.

item.title: Elasticity of Demand
item.description: Price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to price, and so how revenue moves when a price changes.

item.title: Utility and the Budget Constraint
item.description: Utility measures the satisfaction a consumer gets from a bundle, while the budget constraint marks what is affordable; the best bundle equalizes marginal utility per yuan.

item.title: Production and Cost
item.description: A production function turns inputs into output, and costs depend on output and input prices. This article covers short-run cost and output decisions only. Marginal cost decides whether one more unit is worth making; average variable cost decides whether to shut down in the short run, and average total cost whether the price covers all costs.

item.title: Competition and Monopoly
item.description: A perfectly competitive firm takes the market price and produces where price equals marginal cost; a monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve, restricts output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost and charges a higher price.

item.title: Externalities and Public Goods
item.description: Externalities are effects on third parties that prices do not reflect, while public goods are nonexcludable and non-rival; both make market provision diverge from the efficient quantity.

item.title: GDP and National Accounts
item.description: GDP is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country in a period; production, income, and expenditure measures should give the same total.

item.title: Nominal and Real Values
item.description: Nominal values use current prices, while real values are adjusted with a price index; only real values support comparisons of quantities across periods.

item.title: Price Indices and Inflation
item.description: A price index tracks the cost of a fixed basket, and inflation is its percentage change; the index level itself is not the inflation rate.

item.title: Employment and Unemployment
item.description: The unemployment rate divides the unemployed by the labor force, not by the whole population; it misses people who stop looking and people who want more hours.

item.title: Consumption and Saving
item.description: Consumption is household spending on final goods and services, and saving is disposable income not consumed; the saving rate measures that split, not a bank balance at a point in time.

item.title: Investment and Capital Formation
item.description: Capital formation measures acquisitions less disposals of produced assets on a gross basis, including fixed capital formation, inventories and valuables; only net capital formation equals an increase in the productive capital stock. National-accounts investment is fixed investment plus inventory change plus net acquisitions of valuables, and net investment subtracts depreciation, so positive gross investment does not guarantee a larger capital stock.

item.title: Growth and Productivity
item.description: Growth comes from more inputs or more output per input; sustained gains in output per person depend on labor productivity, not longer hours alone.

item.title: The Business Cycle
item.description: The business cycle alternates expansion and contraction; a recession runs from peak to trough, and the dates are usually assigned after the fact.

item.title: Monetary Policy Transmission
item.description: Monetary policy affects aggregate demand through interest rates, credit, asset prices, exchange rates, and expectations, with lags and leakages from the policy rate to output and inflation.

item.title: Fiscal Policy and the Multiplier
item.description: Fiscal policy affects aggregate demand through spending and taxes; the multiplier magnifies an initial change in spending, but leakages, crowding out, and supply limits constrain it.

item.title: The Balance of Payments
item.description: The balance of payments records all economic transactions between a country's residents and nonresidents in a period; a current account deficit is matched by net foreign capital inflow.

item.title: Exchange-Rate Regimes and the Open Economy
item.description: An exchange-rate regime determines whether the nominal rate is set by the market, a rule, or official intervention; the core tradeoff is between exchange-rate stability and monetary policy independence.

item.title: Comparative Advantage and Trade
item.description: Comparative advantage ranks producers by opportunity cost, not absolute productivity; even when one side is more efficient in every good, specialization and trade can benefit both.

item.title: Income Distribution and Inequality
item.description: Income distribution describes how income is spread across households; quintile shares, the Lorenz curve, and the Gini coefficient measure inequality, but definitions shape the conclusion.

item.title: Games and Information
item.description: When outcomes depend on others' choices and one side knows more than the other, game theory and information economics provide testable equilibrium and contracting benchmarks.

item.title: Labor, Population and Education
item.description: Labor markets connect population, skills, migration and family decisions; wages and returns to education emerge from those forces together.

item.title: Industry, Innovation and the Digital Economy
item.description: Innovation links R&D, diffusion, intellectual property and competition policy; the digital economy changes cost structures, network effects and how markets are entered.

item.title: Cities, Regions and Space
item.description: Urban and regional economics puts distance, density and land in one framework: agglomeration brings efficiency, while congestion and land rents bring costs.

item.title: Environment, Energy and Agriculture
item.description: Environmental, energy and agricultural problems share a structure: resource use creates external costs, prices and property rights allocate them, and natural conditions limit how fast substitution can occur.

item.title: Behavior, Experiments and Public Services
item.description: Behavioral economics corrects the standard model with observable biases, while experiments and public services turn those biases into testable, retractable policy tools.

item.title: Law, Organizations and Comparative Economies
item.description: Law and organizations decide who bears costs and who holds decision rights; comparative economics tests those rules across institutional traditions.

item.title: China and the Global Economy
item.description: China's relationship with the global economy is shaped by trade, investment, supply chains and institutional choices; no single indicator captures it.

item.title: Education Returns, Population Structure and Labour Participation
item.description: Education raises productivity and participation, but returns depend on quality, matching, demography and measurement bias; a credential premium alone is not enough.

item.title: Information Asymmetry, Signaling and Mechanism Design
item.description: When one side knows more, prices and contracts distort; signaling, screening and incentives try to reveal information through verifiable costs.

item.title: Economies of Scale, Economies of Scope and Capacity Utilization
item.description: Economies of scale come from spreading fixed costs over more output and from specialization; economies of scope come from sharing capabilities across products, and capacity utilization measures how far actual output is from sustainable maximum output. All three can lower cost, but all have limits: coordination cost, weak demand and quality loss can make “bigger” more expensive.

item.title: Market Concentration, Entry Barriers and Platform Competition
item.description: Market concentration describes how shares are distributed, entry barriers describe why new rivals struggle to enter, and platform competition adds network effects, multi-homing and switching costs to the same picture. High concentration does not automatically mean high prices, and low concentration does not automatically mean effective competition; market boundaries, entry conditions and actual conduct matter.

item.title: Growth Accounting: Capital Deepening, Human Capital and TFP
item.description: Growth accounting splits output growth into capital, labour, human capital and total factor productivity. It answers whether growth comes mainly from more inputs or from using inputs more efficiently, but it cannot treat the TFP residual as pure technological progress; measurement error, utilization, allocation and rents all sit inside it.

item.title: Externalities, Pigouvian Taxes and Cap-and-Trade: When Price Tools Work
item.description: Externalities let private cost omit social cost. A Pigouvian tax puts a price on the damage and feeds it back into decisions, while cap-and-trade fixes the quantity of emissions and lets the permit price adjust. Both can correct overproduction, but price certainty and quantity certainty cannot both be guaranteed; damage measurement, leakage and transaction cost decide when they work.

item.title: Monetary Policy Transmission: Interest-Rate, Credit and Balance-Sheet Channels
item.description: Monetary policy does not attach the policy rate directly to every borrower. It travels through funding cost, credit conditions, asset prices, the exchange rate and expectations to spending and inflation. Transmission is lagged, leaky and weakened by fixed-rate debt, bank capital and supply shocks.

item.title: Fiscal Multipliers: Spending, Taxes and Automatic Stabilizers
item.description: The fiscal multiplier is not a fixed constant. It is the feedback chain from a first-round shock to income, consumption and further income, reduced by leakages. Government purchases, tax cuts and transfers have different multipliers; automatic stabilizers cushion downturns, while openness, debt constraints and supply bottlenecks change the result.

item.title: Tariffs, Quotas and Trade Agreements: The Welfare Ledger of Trade Barriers
item.description: Tariffs and quotas both raise domestic prices, but tariff revenue goes to the government while quota rents go to licence holders. Trade agreements lower barriers among members while retaining rules costs. The welfare ledger must separate consumer losses, producer gains, fiscal revenue and efficiency losses.

item.title: Property Rights, State Capacity and the Institutional Conditions for Development
item.description: Property rights lower the risk that an investment will be seized, while state capacity determines whether rules are enforced and whether taxes become public goods. Institutions are not abstract labels but a checklist: registration, contract enforcement, revenue collection, commitment and accountability.

item.title: R&D, Diffusion and Platforms: Returns and Limits of Innovation Policy
item.description: Social returns to R&D often exceed private returns, so knowledge spillovers leave private investment below the social optimum. Patents, subsidies, public research and standards are different tools. Platforms and AI add network effects, data and scale, changing how innovation gains are distributed; policy must weigh incentives, diffusion and entry together.

item.title: Land, Commuting and Housing: The Price Ledger of Spatial Equilibrium
item.description: Urban space is priced by three ledgers at once: access to jobs, the cost of commuting and congestion, and how housing supply responds to price. Put rent gradients, commuting costs and supply elasticity together, and the same urban growth can show up as higher prices in one city and longer commutes and lower density in another.

item.title: Carbon Prices, Allowances and Abatement Costs: The Allocation Ledger of Climate Policy
item.description: A carbon tax fixes the emissions price; an emissions trading system fixes the emissions total. Both push firms to abate where it is cheapest, but how allowances are allocated, how revenue is used and whether emissions leak decide who bears the cost behind the same carbon price. Climate policy is not a choice of tool name; it is an alignment of marginal abatement cost, coverage and complementary policy.

item.title: Defaults, Nudges and Public Services: Effects and Limits of Behavioral Interventions
item.description: Defaults and reminders can raise participation in public services, but effects found in a trial are not the effects that survive scale-up. Put average treatment effect, unit cost, sample size, persistence and spillovers on one ledger to judge whether an intervention is worth scaling or only works in a small setting.

item.title: Credit Relationships
item.description: A credit relationship moves purchasing power across time under contract: the lender gives up funds now, and the borrower promises to repay principal and interest later. Enforceability, information and collateral decide whether the relationship works.

item.title: Bank Balance Sheets
item.description: A bank balance sheet lists reserves, loans and securities as assets and deposits and borrowings as liabilities, with equity as the difference; it shows that banks operate mainly with other people's money, and it explains why deposits are not the bank's own funds.

item.title: Deposits, Lending and Credit Creation
item.description: When a bank makes a loan it credits an equal deposit to the borrower, so money is created; credit creation is limited by reserves, capital, liquidity and loan demand, and the money multiplier is an upper bound rather than a forecast.

item.title: Central Bank Balance Sheets
item.description: A central bank balance sheet lists securities, lending and foreign reserves as assets and currency in circulation and bank reserves as liabilities; it records how the monetary base is created and shows why a central bank does not need deposits before expanding.

item.title: Reserves and Liquidity
item.description: Reserves are balances that banks hold at the central bank, while liquidity is a bank's ability to pay on time without unacceptable losses; reserves are only one layer of liquidity, and reserve requirements are no substitute for liquidity regulation.

item.title: Payment, Clearing and Settlement
item.description: Payment starts a transfer of value, clearing reconciles instructions and calculates what participants owe, and settlement completes the transfer with central bank money or eligible assets; netting saves liquidity but concentrates credit and liquidity risk in the clearing arrangement.

item.title: Custody and Asset Rights
item.description: Custody hands safekeeping, settlement and record-keeping to a specialist institution, but it does not by itself change beneficial ownership; segregation and the ability to exercise rights depend on the account structure, the agreement and applicable law.

item.title: Simple and Compound Interest
item.description: Simple interest is charged only on principal, while compound interest adds interest to principal and earns interest on it; the same rate and horizon can produce different future values and effective annual rates depending on the method and compounding frequency.

item.title: Present Value and Discounted Cash Flows
item.description: Present value converts future cash flows to today at a discount rate, and discounted cash flow sums those present values; the rate, timing and cash-flow assumptions jointly determine the result.

item.title: Interest-Rate Types and Conventions
item.description: A quoted rate means little without its compounding, annualization and risk conventions; compare rates only on a consistent basis.

item.title: Risk Premium
item.description: A risk premium is the expected return above the risk-free rate; it compensates non-diversifiable risk, not every kind of volatility.

item.title: The Law of One Price and No-Arbitrage
item.description: Identical claims to future cash flows should have the same price; no-arbitrage turns that constraint into a pricing benchmark, though frictions let deviations persist.

item.title: Introduction to Asset Pricing Models
item.description: Asset pricing models map systematic risk to a required return, which is then used to discount cash flows; CAPM is the simplest one-factor benchmark.

item.title: Cost of Capital
item.description: The cost of capital is the return investors require to supply funds and the hurdle rate for projects; the weighted average cost of capital combines after-tax debt and equity costs at market-value weights and applies only to comparable-risk projects.

item.title: The Accounting Equation
item.description: Assets equal liabilities plus equity. The identity explains how resources are financed, but it does not mean assets are worth their market value or that a company is safe.

item.title: The Income Statement
item.description: The income statement summarizes revenue, expenses and profit over a period on an accrual basis; net income is not cash flow, and readers should separate gross profit, operating income and one-off items.

item.title: The Cash-Flow Statement
item.description: The cash-flow statement reports cash receipts and payments over a period in operating, investing and financing activities, and reconciles net income to operating cash flow under the indirect method; it complements the income statement but does not by itself establish a company's value.

item.title: Accrual Accounting
item.description: Accrual accounting recognizes revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, not when cash changes hands; it improves comparability across periods but relies on estimates, so profit and cash flow can diverge.

item.title: Sources of Corporate Finance
item.description: Companies fund assets with internal retained earnings or external debt and equity; the sources differ in claims, cost, control and maturity, and the choice should fit the target capital structure.

item.title: Capital Structure
item.description: Capital structure is the relative share of debt and equity financing; in perfect markets leverage does not change firm value, while tax shields and financial distress costs jointly set a target debt level.

item.title: Dividends and Buybacks
item.description: Dividends pay profit to shareholders in proportion to their holdings, while buybacks use cash to repurchase shares and cut the share count; both return cash but differ in per-share effects, execution rules and disclosure.

item.title: Corporate Governance and Conflicts of Interest
item.description: Corporate governance allocates rights and accountability among shareholders, the board, management and stakeholders; independent directors, committees, related-party disclosure and voting constrain conflicts of interest but do not eliminate agency costs.

item.title: Introduction to Finance
item.description: Finance is not about money making money; it rearranges savings, risk, maturity and information between surplus and deficit units.

item.title: Financial Institutions
item.description: Financial institutions differ not by sign but by balance sheet, maturity transformation, revenue source and regulatory perimeter.

item.title: Insurance and Pension Systems
item.description: Insurance and pensions are both intertemporal risk arrangements: one pools uncertain individual losses into a priceable pool, the other moves income from working life to retirement.

item.title: The International Financial System
item.description: The international financial system is a cross-border arrangement of payments, credit and reserves; its efficiency comes from networks, and so does its fragility.

item.title: Foundations of Digital Finance
item.description: Digital finance changes the technology layer of payments and settlement, but the liability, credit risk and legal rights of money still have to be identified item by item.

item.title: Financial Stability
item.description: Financial stability is the system's ability to keep payments, saving, borrowing and investment working through a shock without cascading failures, not the absence of volatility.

item.title: Regulation, Law and Ethics
item.description: Financial regulation protects enforceable rights and market integrity; ethics addresses judgment where the rulebook runs out.

item.title: Financial Institution Balance Sheets and Maturity/Credit Transformation
item.description: Financial institutions turn short-term liabilities into long-term assets, bearing maturity, credit and liquidity risk; capital and liquidity buffers determine how much shock they can absorb.

item.title: Early Economic Thought
item.description: From Aristotle to Aquinas, early economic thought asked how households acquire goods, when exchange is fair, and why interest is suspect; this article reads the primary texts in context and marks the limits of interpretation.

item.title: Mercantilism and Physiocracy
item.description: Mercantilism and physiocracy both asked where wealth comes from and what the state should do, but answered differently; this article compares their contexts, texts, criticisms and later misreadings.

item.title: Classical Political Economy
item.description: From Smith and Malthus to Ricardo, classical political economy asked how wealth grows, what determines value, and how output is divided; this article reads the primary texts in context and marks the limits of interpretation.

item.title: The Formation of Marxist Economics
item.description: From the 1848 Manifesto to Capital Volume I in 1867, Marx analysed capitalism as a historical system; this article traces the texts, core arguments, debates and later misreadings.

item.title: The Marginal Revolution and Neoclassical Economics
item.description: From the 1870s, Jevons, Menger and Walras shifted value theory toward marginal utility, and Marshall combined utility, cost and time; this article sets out the claims, evidence and limits of that change.

item.title: The Keynesian Revolution and Postwar Debates
item.description: From the monetary debates of the 1920s through the General Theory, the Employment Act of 1946, the Phillips curve and stagflation, this article examines the texts, policies and disputes of the Keynesian revolution, distinguishing Keynes himself from later "Keynesianism".

item.title: Institutional, Behavioral and Pluralist Traditions
item.description: From Veblen's critique of institutions to Simon's bounded rationality, Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory and Ostrom's polycentric governance, this article shows how these traditions challenge the rational-actor model, and sets out the method and the limits of each.

item.title: Agriculture, Commerce and Early Markets
item.description: From Domesday (1086) to eighteenth-century agricultural commercialisation, this article examines how farming, trade and market institutions evolved in Europe, mainly England, and where continuity and rupture lie.

item.title: The Industrial Revolution and Long-Run Growth
item.description: From eighteenth-century British technology and factories to cross-country catch-up by 1913, this article asks why the Industrial Revolution happened, how growth accelerated, and where the "revolution" narrative strains against long-run statistics.

item.title: Globalization, Trade and Divergence
item.description: From Ricardo to twenty-first-century trade openness, this article examines how globalization widened and then partly narrowed income gaps between countries, separating theoretical gains from historical distribution.

item.title: Economic Institutions and Commerce in Imperial China
item.description: From Northern Song paper money to Ming-Qing silver taxation, this article examines land, money and market institutions in imperial China and the tension between state capacity and commercial expansion.

item.title: China's Modern Economic Transition
item.description: From the five treaty ports of 1842 to the renminbi of 1948, this article examines how treaty tariffs, modern industry and currency unification reshaped China's economy, and where the statistics and interpretations end.

item.title: China's Modern Industrialization
item.description: From 12 billion yuan of industrial value added in 1952 to 31.7% of GDP in 2023, this article examines the stages of Chinese industrialization, the statistical definitions, and the efficiency questions behind output.

item.title: Reform, Opening and Market Development
item.description: From 1978 to 2023, this article examines how reform and opening widened markets and changed trade and growth, and how policy, data and interpretation should be kept apart.

item.title: The Evolution of Monetary Systems
item.description: From commodity money and coinage to convertible paper and fiat money, how issuers, redemption promises and credibility changed.

item.title: A History of Banking and Central Banks
item.description: From Stockholms Banco to the Bank Charter Act and the creation of the Federal Reserve, this article covers the verifiable milestones, changing functions and early constraints of banking and central-bank institutions.

item.title: Public Debt and Fiscal History
item.description: How war, taxation and growth shaped public debt levels and debt management in Britain and the United States, from the late seventeenth century to 2025.

item.title: Gold Standard, Bretton Woods and Floating Rates
item.description: From the classical gold standard to Bretton Woods and the closing of the gold window in 1971, how fixed rates, convertibility and adjustment changed.

item.title: A History of Joint-Stock Companies and Securities Markets
item.description: From the Bank of England's charter in 1694 and the South Sea Bubble to the 1792 Buttonwood Agreement and the 1929 crash, how companies, exchanges and regulation shaped one another.

item.title: A History of Funds, Indices and Investment Thought
item.description: From the first U.S. open-end mutual fund in 1924 to the first index fund for individual investors in 1976, how indices, funds and investment ideas reinforced one another; the disputed start year of the price averages could not be checked against a source and is kept only as this article's note.

item.title: A History of Futures, Options and Risk Transfer
item.description: From the Chicago Board of Trade in 1848 to the CFTC in 1974 and options on futures in 1982, showing how standard contracts, margin and clearing made price risk tradable.

item.title: Reading Bubbles and Crises Comparatively
item.description: Comparing 1929 and 2008 starts with what was knowable at the time, then examines mechanisms, institutions, policy and outcomes rather than drawdown alone.

item.title: Regional and Comparative History
item.description: Regional and comparative history places experiences from different continents under the same questions; the point is not who came first but how conditions, institutions and measurement differ.

item.title: Commons Governance and Institutional Analysis
item.description: Common-pool resources are not solved only by nationalisation or privatisation; boundaries, rules, monitoring and graduated sanctions can support polycentric governance.

item.title: Comparing Bubbles: 1637, 1720, 1929 and 2008
item.description: Four famous bubbles differ in assets, leverage and institutions; compare mechanisms, not overlaid price curves.

item.title: Real Returns and Purchasing Power
item.description: Convert net nominal return into real return with the Fisher relation, and put fees, taxes and inflation in one calculation chain; all example numbers are hypothetical.

item.title: Choosing an Investment Benchmark
item.description: Choose the reference from goals and investable range first, then align return, fee and frequency conventions; all example numbers are hypothetical and a market index itself cannot be bought.

item.title: Building an Investment Research Process
item.description: Turn an opinion into a traceable, falsifiable research file: state the question and falsification conditions, then check the 10-K, 8-K and EDGAR source documents; all example numbers are hypothetical.

item.title: Macro Scenario Analysis
item.description: Turn a macro view into reproducible conditional paths: baseline, inflation-upside and recession cases mapped to portfolio exposures; all example numbers are hypothetical, not forecasts or advice.

item.title: Industry Competition and Business Models
item.description: Judge whether profits can persist through industry structure, unit economics and capital returns: start with the profit pool and entry barriers, then compute customer lifetime value and acquisition-cost payback; all example numbers are hypothetical.

item.title: Earnings-Quality Analysis
item.description: Judge whether reported profit is sustainable, cash-backed and comparable: reconcile net income to operating cash flow, then explain the gap through accruals, revenue quality, non-GAAP adjustments and notes; all example numbers are hypothetical.

item.title: Cash-Flow Valuation: A Research Process
item.description: Estimate a value range from future free cash flow, a discount rate and a terminal value: rebuild base cash flow, discount each year, then sensitize; all example numbers are hypothetical.

item.title: Comparability in Relative Valuation
item.description: The hard part of relative valuation is comparability, not the multiple: define the question and peer set, align dates, capital structure and accounting, then explain differences; all example numbers are hypothetical.

item.title: Reverse Valuation and Expectations
item.description: Treat the market price as given and solve for the growth or return it implies, then test whether those expectations are credible; all example numbers are hypothetical.

item.title: Valuation Sensitivity and Scenarios
item.description: Test how much a valuation conclusion depends on its key assumptions using sensitivity tables and probability-weighted scenarios; all example numbers are hypothetical.

item.title: Trend, Price and Volume
item.description: Use moving averages, closes and volume to test whether a trend exists, while stating lag, false breakouts and out-of-sample checks; the example is hypothetical data.

item.title: Common Technical Indicators: Calculation and Limits
item.description: Recompute SMA, EMA, MACD and the stochastic oscillator from the same hypothetical prices to show parameter effects, lag and conflicting signals.

item.title: Economic Interpretation of Factor Strategies
item.description: Use a hypothetical 12-month value factor series to show how factor portfolios are built, where returns may come from and how costs test the story, separating statistical from economic significance.

item.title: Interpreting Backtest Results
item.description: Use a hypothetical 60-month backtest to separate statistical significance, trading costs, multiple trials and out-of-sample evidence, so a historical fit is not mistaken for a future return.

item.title: Diversification and Common Risk
item.description: Diversification reduces idiosyncratic risk but cannot remove the market and recession risks shared by all assets.

item.title: Asset Allocation and Risk Budgeting
item.description: Use a two-asset hypothetical example to distinguish capital weights from risk contributions, compute volatility, marginal risk contribution and risk budgets, and show the limits imposed by leverage, correlation and estimation error.

item.title: Position Sizing and Rebalancing
item.description: Use a hypothetical CNY 1 million portfolio to size a position from a risk budget, trigger rebalancing at a 5 percentage point drift, and calculate the trade, cost and resulting exposure.

item.title: Hedging: Purpose and Cost
item.description: Use a hypothetical coffee purchase to show how futures and options lock a price, surrender part of the upside and leave basis risk, and how margin, financing, fees and basis change the effective price.

item.title: Performance Evaluation and Attribution
item.description: Compare a hypothetical 8.7% portfolio return with a 6.8% benchmark, deduct a 0.60% fee, and decompose the 1.30 percentage point net excess into allocation, selection and interaction effects while showing why one year cannot prove skill.

item.title: Trade Execution and Slippage
item.description: Use a hypothetical 20,000-share buy to compare a CNY 50.00 decision price with a CNY 50.18 average fill, splitting 36 basis points of slippage, 3 basis points of commission and a 39 basis point implementation shortfall, and show the fill risk of a limit order.

item.title: Behavioral Biases and an Investment Journal
item.description: Use a hypothetical journal of 30 decisions to record ex ante reasons, invalidation conditions and bias tags, then review adherence, holding-period gaps and outcome gaps instead of judging decision quality by profit alone.

item.title: Household Wealth and Retirement Planning
item.description: Use a hypothetical 40-year-old couple's balance sheet to convert a 70% replacement rate, 2.5% inflation and 25-year retirement into CNY 4.64 million of required assets, compare it with CNY 5.53 million projected, and show why a 119% funding ratio is not secure under return and longevity stress.

item.title: Investment Strategies
item.description: An investment strategy is not a style label but a reproducible set of return sources, risk exposures, capacity limits and trading costs.

item.title: Responsible Investing and Professional Practice
item.description: Responsible investing brings environmental, social and governance information into due diligence and portfolio constraints; professional practice puts suitability, conflicts and client assets where they can be checked.

item.title: Transaction Cost Analysis: Impact, Slippage and VWAP/TWAP
item.description: Trading cost is not just a commission; it is the gap between the decision price and execution price, made of delay, spread, impact and opportunity cost.

item.title: Common and Preferred Shares
item.description: Both are equity claims on the same company, but voting power, dividend priority, liquidation order and exit terms differ under the charter and offering documents.

item.title: Bond Rights and Cash Flows
item.description: A bond is a debt claim; holders receive coupons and principal under the offering documents, while coupon, price, yield and risk are distinct ideas.

item.title: Indices and Investment Benchmarks
item.description: An index is a rules-based measure of market performance, not a directly held product; a benchmark is the reference used to judge a portfolio, and both must be checked for method and basis.

item.title: Fund Structures
item.description: Funds pool investor money under a contract; legal form, share rights, valuation and exit mechanics matter more than the label.

item.title: ETF Creation, Redemption and Premiums
item.description: ETFs trade at market prices while authorized participants create and redeem shares in creation units, usually priced at NAV; arbitrage usually narrows premiums but does not guarantee it.

item.title: Bank Wealth-Management and Trust Products
item.description: Bank wealth-management and trust products are non-principal-guaranteed asset-management products with different issuers, legal relationships, investor thresholds, exit rules and disclosure requirements.

item.title: Comparing Ways to Hold Gold
item.description: Physical gold, gold ETFs and gold futures all provide gold exposure, but their legal claims, cash flows, leverage and risks differ.

item.title: Silver's Industrial and Investment Roles
item.description: Silver is consumed by electronics, photovoltaics and brazing, and also held as an investment; industrial and investment demand together affect its price and risks.

item.title: Copper and Industrial Metals
item.description: Copper underlies construction, power grids, transport and electronics; physical metal, futures and mining shares carry different rights and risks.

item.title: The Steel Supply Chain
item.description: From iron ore, coking coal and scrap to crude steel, hot-rolled coil and rebar, cash flows, costs and risks pass through each processing stage.

item.title: Crude Oil and Refined Products
item.description: Crude oil is refinery feedstock and refined products are its outputs; crude futures, product futures and refining margins carry different rights and cash flows.

item.title: Natural Gas and Electricity Markets
item.description: Natural gas is a storable, transportable commodity, while electricity is a secondary energy source that must be balanced in real time; their contracts, costs and risks differ.

item.title: Grains, Oilseeds and Agricultural Supply
item.description: Grains and oilseeds are priced by variety, grade and delivery period; weather, stocks, crush margins and basis shape the cash flows and risks of the agricultural chain.

item.title: Soft Commodities and Livestock
item.description: Coffee, cocoa, sugar and cotton respond to origin weather and grading, while cattle and hogs respond to biological cycles and feed costs; their contracts and delivery differ.

item.title: FX Quotes and Trading Instruments
item.description: FX is quoted in currency pairs; spot, forward, swap, futures and option instruments carry different rights, cash flows, margin and counterparty risks.

item.title: Futures Contracts and Margin
item.description: Futures are exchange-standardized contracts; both sides post margin and are marked to market daily, so leverage, margin calls and delivery rules shape losses and exits.

item.title: Options: Rights, Obligations and Payoffs
item.description: An option buyer pays a premium for a right, while the writer receives the premium and owes performance; strike, premium and expiry price determine the payoff.

item.title: Swaps and Structured Products
item.description: Swaps exchange cash flows rather than principal, while structured products combine debt with derivative terms; both depend on counterparties, collateral and offering documents.

item.title: Real Estate and REITs
item.description: Real estate can be owned directly or through REITs; a REIT's tax status depends on distribution, shareholder and asset tests, and listed and non-traded shares differ sharply in liquidity.

item.title: Private Equity, Private Credit and Hedge Funds
item.description: Hedge funds typically admit only accredited investors, and private credit funds are mostly closed-end and not open to retail investors; like private equity they are limited in liquidity, but their assets, leverage, cash flows and exit routes differ.

item.title: Insurance and Retirement Products
item.description: Insurance and retirement products both manage long-term risk, but insurance transfers specific event risk while retirement accounts provide tax and savings arrangements; they are not substitutes.

item.title: Digital Assets and Digital Finance
item.description: Digital assets are not one asset class; tokens, stablecoins, DeFi positions and central bank digital currencies differ in legal rights, custody and risk.

item.title: Chemicals, Rubber and Materials
item.description: Chemicals, rubber and materials are intermediate-goods markets linking energy, manufacturing and construction; prices reflect capacity cycles, feedstock costs and logistics radius.

item.title: Environmental, Freight and Specialty Markets
item.description: Environmental and freight markets trade rights, capacity or services rather than standardised goods; standards, compliance and market depth determine whether prices can be interpreted.

item.title: Retirement Products and Accounts
item.description: Retirement products have three layers: account rules, product structure and decumulation; a change in any layer changes final income and risk.

item.title: Collectibles and Other Alternatives
item.description: Alternative collectibles are priced through authenticity, rights, custody and liquidity; without enforceable rights and verifiable provenance, a price is only a story.

item.title: Chemical Value Chains: Feedstock, Spreads and Inventory
item.description: Chemical value is set not by one price but by spreads across feedstock, processing, grade, region and inventory.

item.title: Collectibles: Valuation, Authenticity and Liquidity
item.description: Collectible prices reflect scarcity, provenance and demand, but authenticity, transaction costs and exit liquidity determine what a buyer actually gets.

item.title: Futures Basis, Rolls and Delivery
item.description: The gap between futures and spot, the cost of rolling and delivery rules jointly determine hedging and holding returns; a futures price move alone is not enough.

item.title: FX Regimes, NDFs and Cross-Border Hedging
item.description: The exchange-rate regime determines which tools are available; NDFs cash-settle around delivery restrictions, but basis, regulation and counterparty risk remain.

item.title: Option Pricing and the Volatility Surface
item.description: Option prices separate direction, time, volatility and rates; implied volatilities across strikes and expiries form a surface.

item.title: Index Construction: Free Float and Benchmark Selection
item.description: An index is not the market itself but a replicable set of eligibility, weighting, capping and rebalancing rules; benchmark choice changes attribution.

item.title: Equity Financing, Governance and Shareholder Rights
item.description: Equity financing trades ownership for capital; dilution, voting, preferences and governance terms determine what existing holders give up.

item.title: Swap Pricing and Structured Tranching
item.description: A swap exchanges two cash-flow streams; a structured product then slices underlying assets into different priority claims. Pricing centres on net present value, counterparty and terms.

item.title: Credit Spreads, Duration and Recovery
item.description: Credit bonds yield more than risk-free rates to compensate default, uncertain recovery, liquidity and terms; duration amplifies rate and spread moves.

item.title: Stablecoins, Custody and On-Chain Settlement Risk
item.description: A stablecoin is an issuer liability, not a bank deposit; reserves, redemption rights, custody and on-chain finality determine whether it holds its peg under stress.

item.title: Frequency and Time Alignment
item.description: Series at different frequencies must first share a reference period and an information set; aggregation is usually safer than disaggregation, and release times and time zones can change the date.

item.title: Seasonal Adjustment and Revisions
item.description: Seasonal adjustment strips out calendar-driven swings, and the adjusted numbers are themselves revised; a monthly change smaller than the typical revision is not yet evidence of a trend.

item.title: Axes, Dual Axes and Misleading Charts
item.description: Axes map values to positions, so changing an axis range or adding a second vertical axis can manufacture crossings and co-movement without touching the data.

item.title: Indexing, Logarithms and Growth Rates
item.description: An index turns a level into a ratio to a base period, and a logarithm turns that ratio into additive changes; growth rates, compound annual growth and doubling times are comparable only when definitions, base periods and price bases match.

item.title: Missing Data, Outliers and Sample Selection
item.description: The same average growth rate changes with who is sampled, who responds, how missing values are filled and how outliers are treated; reporting the rule and a sensitivity range is more honest than reporting one precise number.

item.title: A Reproducible Research Workflow
item.description: Reproducibility is not “the code ran once”; it means another person can take the data version, code, environment and documentation and recompute the same table with one command. It guarantees recomputation, not correctness.

item.title: Probability Distributions, Expectation and Variance
item.description: A probability distribution assigns a probability to each possible outcome; expectation is the long-run average, while variance and standard deviation measure dispersion. They describe an assumed distribution, not the next outcome.

item.title: Covariance and Correlation
item.description: Covariance and correlation describe linear co-movement. They do not identify causation and cannot replace checks on samples, timing and outliers.

item.title: Sampling and Confidence Intervals
item.description: A confidence interval combines a sample mean with sampling error to give a range for the population mean; 95% means about 95% of intervals from repeated samples would cover the mean, not that this interval has a 95% probability of containing it.

item.title: Hypothesis Testing and Practical Significance
item.description: Hypothesis testing treats “no difference” as the null and asks whether the sample supports rejecting it; a small p-value means the data are inconsistent with the null, not that the effect is large, important or real.

item.title: Introduction to Linear Regression
item.description: Linear regression summarizes the average relationship between two variables with a line; slope, intercept and R-squared describe the sample, while significance and causal interpretation depend on design, assumptions and the limits of the evidence.

item.title: Control Variables and Confounding
item.description: Control variables are used to block confounding paths, not to include every available variable; a simple association can shrink after adjustment, but adjustment itself can introduce new bias.

item.title: Causality and Identification
item.description: Causal identification is not a significant regression; it maps observed data to a counterfactual through design or assumptions. Random experiments provide a benchmark, while observational methods each carry their own conditions.

item.title: Trends, Nonstationarity and Spurious Regression
item.description: Two nonstationary series with their own trends can produce a high R-squared and a significant slope even when they are independent; level-regression significance must be read alongside trends, autocorrelation and differenced results.

item.title: Leads, Lags and Forecasting
item.description: Cross-correlation and lagged regression can describe which series moves first, but transformations, windows and multiple tests all manufacture “leads”; forecasting skill must be judged by out-of-sample error.

item.title: Rolling Analysis and Structural Change
item.description: With 0.54 estimated in the first half and 0.20 in the second, a full-sample slope of 0.34 hides the break; rolling paths, break tests and out-of-sample forecasts must be reported together, with the window and break date explained - and a test that fails to reject may simply lack power.

item.title: Event-Study Basics
item.description: After removing normal returns with a market model, 40 hypothetical firms show a three-day average cumulative abnormal return of 1.9% with a t value of 4.8; a control window with no injected effect still reads 0.1% in this sample, which is the sampling noise such estimates carry before clustering and model choice are considered.

item.title: Backtesting and Look-Ahead Bias
item.description: A signal that includes the current month’s return earns 20.8% a year, while the version using only data through last month earns 11.4%; look-ahead inflates a constructed result, not skill, and the best of 1000 random strategies does not survive out of sample.

item.title: Survivorship Bias and Trading Costs
item.description: In a simulated 500-fund, 120-month universe, keeping only surviving funds lifts annualized return from 5.7% to 6.6%; a high-turnover strategy earns 9.4% gross but 7.96% after 30 bp one-way costs, only 0.22 percentage points above the low-turnover version.

item.title: Out-of-Sample Testing and Overfitting
item.description: Searching 500 parameter sets over 180 months gives a best in-sample Sharpe of 0.831 that falls to 0.072 out of sample; reusing the out-of-sample window for selection raises the reported value to 1.131, while the same combination falls to 0.489 over the final 60 months.

item.title: Multiple Testing and Data Snooping
item.description: Among 60 simulated rules with no predictive power, 4 look significant at the 5% level; under a Bonferroni threshold of 0.000833 none survive, while the chance of at least one false positive is 95.4%.

item.title: Evidence Hierarchies and Research Reports
item.description: Sampling 12 simulated studies by evidence tier gives realised average effects of 2.4% in tier A, 4.5% in B and 8.2% in C, 4.7% overall and 3.6% excluding the practitioner notes; a report should give tiers, a range and a certainty rating, not one headline number.

item.title: Mathematical Foundations
item.description: Mathematics for research is not a pile of formulas; it turns a question into functions, constraints and computable steps, and tells you when approximations fail.

item.title: Forecasting and Machine Learning
item.description: The core of forecasting and machine learning is not model complexity but time boundaries, baselines, validation and drift monitoring.

item.title: Alternative Data and Complex Systems
item.description: Alternative data and complex systems expand what can be observed while magnifying representativeness, licensing and identification problems; the method's value lies in stating the limits.

item.title: Matrices, Calculus and Numerical Stability
item.description: Matrix operations and calculus underpin quantitative analysis, but conditioning, scaling and floating-point error make the same formula produce different answers.

item.title: Data Versioning, Pipelines and Reproducible Experiments
item.description: Reproduction is not rerunning a notebook; it means fixing data, code, environment and random seeds so every step is auditable.

item.title: Event Studies: Windows, Abnormal Returns and Inference
item.description: An event study subtracts model-expected return from realised return in an event window to obtain abnormal return; window choice and inference determine credibility.

item.title: What Economics Studies
item.description: Economics studies how people choose under scarcity, and how those choices interact at the level of individuals, markets and the whole economy.

item.title: Scarcity and Choice
item.description: Scarcity means wants exceed what is available, so choice is unavoidable; the production possibilities frontier turns that trade-off into a boundary that can be calculated and compared.

item.title: Functions of Money
item.description: Money is what is generally accepted in exchange and settlement. Its roles as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value lower transaction costs, but acceptance and stable value are conditions rather than guarantees.

item.title: The Time Value of Money
item.description: Cash flows at different dates cannot be added directly; compounding moves value forward and discounting brings it back to today.

item.title: How to Read Economic History and the History of Economic Thought
item.description: Reading economic history requires separating primary texts, editions, context and later interpretation; reconstruct what was knowable before judging outcomes or drawing analogies.

item.title: Historical Analogies and Hindsight Bias
item.description: Compare mechanisms, institutions and scale before asking whether “this time looks like then”; outcome knowledge makes the past seem more predictable than it was.

item.title: Writing Investment Goals and Constraints
item.description: Define the goal, amount, horizon, liquidity and risk capacity before discussing asset allocation; a goal statement is not a return promise.

item.title: Return, Risk and Cost Trade-offs
item.description: Compare net nominal return, risk and costs on one basis, using scenario ranges instead of a single expected value; all example numbers are hypothetical.

item.title: Assets and Instruments
item.description: Assets answer what stores value; instruments define the legal claims and cash flows used to hold it, so the same underlying can carry different rights and risks.

item.title: Cash and Money-Market Instruments
item.description: Cash, deposits, Treasury bills, commercial paper, CDs, repos and money market funds all offer short-term liquidity, but their issuers, rights, exits and risks differ.

item.title: Repo, Money Funds and Liquidity Tiers
item.description: Short-term cash instruments all look cash-like, but collateral, redemption, valuation and counterparties differ; liquidity tiers emerge under stress.

item.title: Data Units and Statistical Definitions
item.description: Similar labels can hide different denominators, units, frequencies and seasonal adjustments; check definitions before comparing, and never fill missing values with zero.

item.title: Stocks and Flows
item.description: A stock is a balance at a point in time and a flow is a change over a period; treating a deficit as debt or income as wealth confuses accounting identities with causal claims.
